title: {{NAME}} and the Rustwork Valley
moral: The most powerful machines are nothing without the living things that teach them why kindness matters.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a bright orange mechanic's jumpsuit with silver zip-pockets, a cobalt blue tool belt with gleaming clasps, and sturdy steel-grey boots with orange laces.

pages.content: Rustwork Valley had a smell unlike anywhere else in the world: hot iron, wild mint, and the dry-dust scent of ancient rock. {{NAME}} slid down the valley's entrance slope on his heels, his orange jumpsuit crackling with static, and landed in the centre of the strangest landscape he had ever seen. Enormous robotic dinosaur skeletons stood everywhere, each one built from copper pipes, gear-toothed joints, and panels of hammered brass. Some were as tall as houses. Some were curled up like sleeping dogs. All of them were still, and all of them had gone dark, their eye-ports dim and lightless. But threading between their massive legs, quick as thought, were dozens of real animals: foxes, rabbits, a glossy black crow who regarded {{NAME}} with extraordinary suspicion, and a single tortoise who appeared to be going somewhere very important at maximum tortoise speed. {{NAME}} unclipped his cobalt tool belt and looked around. Somewhere in this valley, the power source had died. He intended to find it.

pages.content: The black crow landed on {{NAME}}'s shoulder with the decisiveness of someone claiming territory. Its name, {{NAME}} learned quickly, was Clank, which seemed unlikely for a bird until it opened its beak and produced a sound exactly like a dropped spanner. Clank had been watching the valley for three days, since the great power-crystal at its centre had gone dark, and the robots had stopped. The robots, Clank explained in a series of clicks and head-tilts that {{NAME}} somehow understood perfectly, had been companions to the animals for generations, helping to clear blocked streams, carry injured creatures to safe ground, and gently herd lost deer back toward the forest. Without them, a family of river otters was stranded on a mud island where the largest stream had silted up and overflowed its banks. {{NAME}}'s eyes widened. He looked at Clank. Clank looked back with the expression of someone who has been waiting for competent assistance and is cautiously relieved it has finally arrived.

pages.content: The power-crystal sat in a cradle at the valley's lowest point, a sphere of pale green glass the size of a football, and its problem was immediately obvious: someone had packed mud into every one of its contact ports. Precise, deliberate mud-packing. A family of very industrious beavers had mistaken it for a particularly smooth and excellent building stone and had incorporated it into a dam. The dam was magnificent. {{NAME}} said so, out loud, because it was true. But he had to open it. He worked fast and careful, extracting the crystal without dismantling the dam itself, rerouting the beaver family to a better stone three metres upstream. Then he sprinted back to the crystal cradle, slammed the sphere into place, and wiped the contacts with the clean corner of his orange sleeve. The valley lit up. Every robot eye-port blazed gold simultaneously. Every copper-and-brass dinosaur head swung upright. The sound was like a cathedral pipe organ played by someone enormously pleased to be awake.

pages.content: The largest robot, a triceratops built from polished bronze with three magnificent spiral horns, walked directly to the flooded stream. It moved with surprising delicacy for something the size of a house, each footfall precise and considered. It pushed its broad armoured head against the collapsed bank and pressed, slowly and steadily, until the mud shifted and the water found its proper channel again. The otter family, four of them, dark and slick and suspicious, edged off their mud island in a careful line. The smallest otter paused at the base of the robot's foot, looked up at the enormous machine, and then patted it twice with one small webbed paw. The robot lowered its bronze head until its cool forehead rested against the ground near the tiny otter. The gesture was unmistakably gentle. {{NAME}} stood absolutely still, tool belt in his hand, and felt something tight in his chest loosen and open like a door swinging wide.

pages.content: By the time the last light left the valley, every animal was settled and every robot was back at its post, their eye-ports glowing a warm, steady amber in the dusk. The tortoise had finally arrived wherever it had been going, and sat there with an air of complete satisfaction. Clank landed on the bronze triceratops's horn and tucked its beak under its wing, the way a bird does when it has decided somewhere is home. {{NAME}} climbed back up the valley slope, his legs aching pleasantly, his tool belt heavy and familiar against his hip. He looked back once. The valley below him glowed like a jar of captured fireflies, warm and alive and quietly content. He curled up at the top of the slope in the soft grass, and the tiredness came at him like a warm wave, carrying him gently under. He was almost asleep when a new sound drifted up from the valley. Not the organ-blast of robots waking. Something smaller. Something singing. One of the machines was making music. {{NAME}} smiled in his sleep and wondered what it was learning to say.
